WE BUILT AN EXTRACTION MACHINE. 
AND CALLED IT PROGRESS? 💎

It's becoming increasingly clear that we are having the wrong argument about AI.

The question is not simply whether AI is good or bad.

The much bigger question is: who benefits?

Alvin Wang Graylin makes a point in this TEDx talk that I think deserves far more attention.

AI is becoming cheaper, more capable and more widely available. That should be extraordinary news. But at the same time, enormous amounts of capital are being poured into a race dominated by a handful of companies, investors and technology giants.

Graylin describes the result as a K-shaped economy: capital goes one way, labour goes the other. The people who own the systems become richer. The people whose work is replaced, reduced or devalued are told that this is simply progress.

I don’t think that is good enough. Do you?

I’m excited about AI. I use it for something every day. As a disabled person, I can already see how transformative it could become when technology finally adapts to me instead of forcing me to adapt to the machines.

We can already see AI improving aspects of medicine, education, accessibility, communication and countless ordinary parts of life.

But if all that increased productivity simply transfers more wealth and power upward, we haven’t created abundance.

WE'VE CREATED AN EXTRAORDINARILY EFFICIENT EXTRACTION MACHINE.

Graylin argues that AI should increasingly be treated as a public good, with regulation, social safety nets and deliberate attempts to distribute its benefits more widely.

That seems to me to be the real political question of AI.

Not whether the machines become intelligent.

Whether we are intelligent enough to decide who they are for.
